content: The World Health Organization (WHO) introduced updated guidelines in 2015 to standardize the measurement of HIV service coverage, gaps, and impact at facility, subnational, and national levels. These guidelines emphasize the use of ten global indicators to monitor the HIV care and treatment cascade, which is essential for tracking the epidemic and the response to it. Six of these indicators rely on data derived from patient diagnosis, testing, and medical records. These six indicators include: 1. The proportion of individuals diagnosed with HIV (knowing their HIV status). 2. Linkage to care. 3. Initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). 4. Retention on ART. 5. Viral load suppression. 6. Mortality. The integration of clinical data into a strategic information framework enables routine measurement of these indicators across facility, subnational, and national levels. In 2017, WHO launched the Consolidated Guidelines on Person-Centred HIV Patient Monitoring and Case Surveillance. These guidelines aim to unify patient monitoring, program monitoring, and surveillance into a single monitoring and evaluation (M&E) system. This approach shifts the focus from counting services delivered to emphasizing individuals and their access to integrated HIV and health services, thereby improving the monitoring of the HIV response. The guidelines highlight three main components: 1. HIV patient monitoring. 2. HIV case surveillance. 3. The use of unique identifiers for person-centred monitoring of HIV services. A key recommendation is to conduct a comprehensive situational analysis as the initial step in transitioning to the collection of person-centred HIV strategic information for patient monitoring and case surveillance. The assessment tool for person-centred HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance provides a structured process for developing a situational analysis of existing HIV strategic information systems, formats, and tools. This tool comprises three components: 1. A document review and information collection tool. 2. A strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis to identify three to five priority actions. 3. A scorecard and priority action plan summarizing key actions and estimating the resources required for implementation. Preliminary assessments conducted in various countries informed the adaptation of the 2017 WHO guidelines. The assessment tool evaluates the current status of patient monitoring and case surveillance systems, identifies opportunities and options, and provides recommendations for next steps, including priority actions and initial cost estimations. The assessment process begins with a stakeholder meeting to review and adapt the data collection tool to the specific needs of the country. The tool is comprehensive and must be tailored to the country’s context. For countries with established systems, the tool evaluates the existing framework. In other countries, it serves as a planning tool to define needs and guide the development and implementation of case surveillance in conjunction with existing patient monitoring and information systems. The assessment involves a desk review of key documents and forms, followed by interviews with key informants and stakeholders at national, subnational, and facility levels. Stakeholders include representatives from the Ministry of Health (MoH), WHO, HIV program officers, monitoring and evaluation (M&E) officers, strategic information (SI) officers, technical working groups on HIV, and partner agencies supporting case surveillance and patient monitoring systems, such as the Global Fund and PEPFAR. The assessment aims to guide the implementation of 15 key recommendations outlined in the guidelines, including: 1. Establishing a minimum dataset for patient care. 2. Transitioning to a treat all approach. 3. Simplifying tools. 4. Enhancing integration and linkages. 5. Conducting data quality reviews and using data to improve care quality. 6. Standardizing core sentinel events and indicators. 7. De-duplicating records to support facilities and improve data quality. 8. Conducting a country situational analysis. 9. Strengthening HIV diagnosis and building on patient monitoring. 10. Collecting data on key populations. 11. Promoting and using unique identifiers. 12. Transitioning from paper-based to electronic patient information systems. 13. Strengthening data security measures. 14. Investing in data systems and ensuring interoperability. 15. Using individual-level data to improve programs and long-term chronic health care. The assessment evaluates the current patient monitoring and HIV surveillance systems, with input from country representatives to adapt tools to the local context. Standardized tools developed for the assessment include: A document review checklist. A document request checklist. An interview guide. A SWOT analysis tool with results. A results scorecard with priority actions and estimated investment requirements. A site visit checklist. A debrief form. The document review checklist (DRvC) for HIV case surveillance involves obtaining and reviewing key documents at least two weeks before the assessment. The team drafts summary paragraphs for each item, which are compiled into a global summary document. The checklist evaluates existing patient-level data collection systems, data flow, reporting systems, policies, strategic plans, and vital registration systems. It also assesses the developmental stage, quality, and functionality of these components. The interview guide (IG) schedules interviews with stakeholders, providing an overview of the assessment and its objectives. For example, stakeholders may be informed that the assessment aims to evaluate the current surveillance system, identify gaps, and develop a prioritized and costed action plan to strengthen individual-level HIV data, case surveillance, and patient monitoring. Interviews may also explore how existing systems function and how they can be adapted to implement the updated 2017 WHO guidelines.
